title: Narrativas de desinformación: impacto, exposición y componente ideológico / Disinformation narratives: Impact, exposure and role of ideology
screen_reason: Nationally distributed online survey of 1,003 Spanish residents aged 18-74 (GESOP, 10-16 March 2023) which, for each of six fact-check-derived disinformation narratives, asked whether the respondent had heard it before. Table 2 reports the share answering yes for every narrative (29% to 73.7%). These are self-reported shares of respondents who encountered specific false claims, i.e. RECALL (exposure), with a stated denominator. The belief/agreement columns and the ideology models are out of scope (belief in false claims does not count), and are not extracted.

estimates.platform: Encuesta online (survey; respondents were also asked which medium or platform they heard it on, but those results are not reported)
estimates.date: Encuesta 10-16 de marzo de 2023; narrativas identificadas a partir de fact-checks del 14 de febrero al 7 de marzo de 2023 / Survey 10-16 March 2023; narratives drawn from fact-checks published 14 February - 7 March 2023
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report having previously heard the disinformation narrative that Poland, Sweden and Norway have sued the WHO accusing it of infecting Europe (N1, 'OMS')
estimates.denominator: 1,003 Spanish residents aged 18-74 surveyed online by GESOP (stratified sampling with uniform allocation: eight sex-by-age strata of 125 interviews each, distributed proportionally by autonomous community and municipality size; margin of error +/- 3.4% at 95% confidence, p=q=0.5)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered 'Sí' to the question of whether they had heard the stated narrative before the survey

(2017), disinformation narratives are false or misleading stories intentionally disseminated with the purpose of deceiving the public"
estimates.page_loc: Tabla 2 'Impacto de las narrativas de desinformación', p. 424 (column 'Exposición a narrativa')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported exposure: respondents said whether they had heard the narrative before. The NARRATIVES themselves were derived from 163 fact-checks published by the Spanish fact-checking organisations Newtral, Maldita and Verificat between 14 February and 7 March 2023, catalogued in an Excel database by keyword and topic; the research team and journalists at Newtral independently grouped the fact-checks into narratives and both arrived at the same six main narratives. So the falsity of the claims rests on fact-checkers, but the exposure measurement itself is unverified self-report, and ground_truth is coded self_report accordingly. No coder-reliability statistic is given for the grouping step.

estimates.notes: topic coded health_other: the claim concerns the WHO being sued for 'infecting Europe', which is COVID-adjacent but never explicitly labelled COVID in the paper, so covid19 was not used. This is the lowest-exposure narrative (29%) and the paper flags it as the one with the strongest belief effect among the exposed (Cramer's V = 0.495). ground_truth is coded self_report (the exposure measure is the respondent's own report); the fact-checker provenance of the six narratives is recorded in ground_truth_detail. source_quote is the paper's Table 2 row for this narrative, the only contiguous verbatim rendering of the value (the surrounding prose sits in interleaved two-column page text).

missed_or_uncertain: (a) The paper reports NO pooled exposure figure across the six narratives, and computing one would be a cross-narrative average barred by R8, so six rows are given rather than one. (b) All 'Acuerdo/total' and 'Acuerdo/exposicion' columns (Table 2) and all of Table 3, Table 4 and Table 5 concern BELIEF in false claims and its association with ideology and prior exposure - explicitly excluded from this review. (c) The survey asked respondents 'de que medio o plataforma la han oido' (from which medium or platform they heard it) and '4) si habian compartido contenido relacionado' (whether they had shared related content). A self-reported sharing share would be a RECALL/sharing row, but NO results for either question are reported anywhere in the text, so nothing can be extracted; this is the most important gap in the paper for this review. (d) The regression tables report 'Observaciones' of 392-415 per narrative rather than 1,003, presumably because neutral (scale point 4) responses are dropped from the binary belief models; the exposure percentages in Table 2 are described as shares 'de los encuestados' (of respondents), so I used N = 1,003 as the denominator. An adjudicator should note that the per-item denominator for exposure is not stated exactly. (e) The 163 fact-checks collected from Newtral, Maldita and Verificat are an all-false corpus with no denominator, so they yield no CONTENT row (explicit exclusion in Sec. 1). (f) Numerous prevalence figures quoted from other studies (Eady et al.: about 1% of Americans exposed to Russian-sponsored disinformation; Grinberg et al.: 6% of political-content sharers got content from fake-news sites, average X user exposed to 1.18% of posts from fake-news sources) are cited from elsewhere and barred by R8.

rob.design: Two-stage design. Stage 1: over three weeks (14 February - 7 March 2023, deliberately outside an electoral period), the team catalogued material identified as disinformation by the three Spanish fact-checking organisations Newtral, Maldita and Verificat, building an Excel database classifying fact-checks by keyword and topic; 163 fact-checks were collected, with the fourth week analysed daily. The research team and journalists from Newtral then independently grouped the fact-checks into narratives and both identified the same six main disinformation narratives. Stage 2: online survey fielded 10-16 March 2023 (kept close in time so respondents would still recall the news), N = 1,003 Spanish residents aged 18-74, fieldwork by GESOP, stratified sampling with uniform allocation across eight sex-by-age strata of 125 interviews each, distributed proportionally within strata by autonomous community and municipality size; margin of error +/- 3.4% at 95% confidence with p=q=0.5. No response rate reported. For each narrative respondents were asked (1) whether they had heard it before, (2) agreement on a 1-7 scale (1 = not true, 7 = true; recoded 1-3 disagree, 4 neutral, 5-7 agree), (3) which medium/platform they heard it on, and (4) whether they had shared related content; only (1) and (2) are reported. Analysis: chi-square tests of independence, Marascuillo multiple-proportion comparisons, and binary logistic regressions (belief as dependent variable, prior exposure and ideology as predictors; McFadden R-squared 0.067-0.197).
